ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The identification of this Source was based on the observation of geomorphological and topographic anomalies constrained by extrapolations from neighbouring faults (Irpinia to the north and Agri Valley to the south).
This Source is associated with the 1857 earthquake following the hypothesis that this event was a complex earthquake involving the rupture of two adjoining fault segments in a short time lapse.
The Melandro-Pergola basin is one of many intermountain depressions filled with lower-middle Pleistocene continental deposits. These were subsequently incised as a result of regional uplift and mildly deformed by a local tectonic source. The pattern of incision suggest the existence of a slight asymmetry of the basin, which exhibits a SW flank steeper than the NE-flank with a depocenter located half-way near the intersection of the Pergola and Melandro rivers (Ponte d'Isca). A characteristic aggrading behaviour is observed along a ca. 5 km stretch of the river. This configuration is compatible with the action of a NW-trending, NE-dipping major fault.
The surface trace of the source has been located coincident with a series of small perched basins and valleys located on top of the mountain ridge that separates the Melandro river valley from the Vallo di Diano to the SW. This topographic feature is continuos for the entire length of the source (i.e. about 18 km) and is well aligned with a similar feature characterising the Maddalena Mts. ridge (i.e. where the Agri Valley source cuts the surface).
The surface expression and long-term deformation of this Source to the NW and of the Agri Valley one to the SW are very similar. In all cases we observed rejuvenation of inherited topography and recent deformation confined along topographic crests.
The width of the source is slightly smaller than that of the two adjacent sources and has been selected using an aspect-ratio criterion based on the assumed source length. Benedetti et al. (1998) hypothesised the presence of Late Quaternary SW-dipping normal faults on the eastern flank of the Vallo di Diano.
These would be part of a larger normal fault system that would include also some SW-dipping normal faults located on the eastern side of the high Agri river valley. According to them this fault system would be the source of the 16 December 1857 earthquake, and the Vallo di Diano segments slipped during a strong foreshock.
The mere existence and the Late Quaternary activity of the SW-dipping Vallo di Diano fault system, that would be formed by two right-stepped segments located right behind the Melandro-Pergola source, is not accepted by all workers. In addition, activity of one of the two would exclude activity of the other.
The 1857 earthquake consisted of two separated shocks, with the second stronger and of longer duration than the first one (Boschi et al., 1995). The most damaged areas were the high Agri Valley between Marsico Nuovo and Montemurro, and the northern termination of the Vallo di Diano near the village of Polla (I=X), west of the high Agri Valley. According to Benedetti et al., this anomalous distribution of damage could be explained with the activation of both the NW-SE trending, SW dipping Agri Valley normal fault system and the Vallo di Diano normal fault system, reaching together a length of about 60 km. This would increase substantially the magnitude expected for this source.
Based on evidence of earthquake complexity, Burrato and Valensise (2008) hypothesized that the 1857 earthquake ruptured in a cascade fashion two adjacent and relatively well-known faults: first the smaller NE-dipping Melandroâ€“Pergola fault, commonly believed to represent a seismic gap between the causative faults of the 1857 and of the 1980 Irpinia (Mw 6:9) earthquakes; and then the larger Agri valley fault proper. Contemporary chronicles reported a time lapse of 2â€“3 min between the two ruptures, thus effectively making them two independent shocks.
The rupture must have proceeded unilaterally from the northwestern edge of the Melandroâ€“Pergola fault, where Mallet placed the earthquake epicenter, thus explaining the concentration of damage â€” and attention by rescue crews and subsequent investigators â€” in the southeastern portion of the High Agri valley.
The epicentral area of the August 19, 1561 earthquake (Me=6.4) falls close to the northern tip of this source. The event heavily struck the northern end of the Vallo di Diano. However, the epicentral location of this event is still debated and has been attributed either to a seismogenic source located on the eastern flank of the Vallo di Diano or to a source in the Melandro river valley (Mucciarelli et al., 1999). The distribution of damage associated with this event does not seem to bear any relationships with the location and geometry of this Source, since the stronger intensities were recorded along a NE-SW trend. Mucciarelli et al. (1999) also demonstrated that high and very high site amplifications can explain the strong damage observed at sites located in the northern Vallo di Diano. Following this observation, the calculation of the source geometry from corrected intensities using the Boxer code (Gasperini et al., 1999) yielded a NE-SW oriented source, which suggests the activation of a transverse lineament (notice that the 1990 Potenza seismic sequence is also somehow related with activity of a more northerly portion of the same lineament).
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Is the northern Vallo di Diano normal fault system active? Is it the source of the strong fore-shock of the 1857 earthquake located to the NW of Val d'Agri as proposed by Benedetti et al. (1998)?
2) Where is the source of the 1561 earthquake located? What is its orientation?
3) Does this Source represent a seismic gap?

pictures.c: Map of historical and instrumental seismicity showing seismic sequenceS that occurred at the boundaries of the main historical earthquake epicentral areas (from Cucci et al. [2004]).

pictures.t: Focal plane solutions and breakout data
pictures.c: Fault plane solutions and breakout data highlighting a NE-SW oriented extensional regime (from Cucci et al. [2004]). The 1990 Potenza seismic sequence was caused by right-lateral faulting on E-W planes.

Epicenter relocations and fault plane solutions of the 1996 and 2002 seismic sequences (from Cucci et al. [2004]). The 1996 sequence occurred close to the southeastern termination of the 1857 seismogenic source, whereas the 2002 sequence bounds the Melandro-Pergola source to the NW.

pictures.t: Summary map of minimum horizontal stress orientation
pictures.c: Summary map of the minimum horizontal stress orientations derived from earthquake focal solutions and breakout data (from Cucci et al. [2004]).
Comparison between the fault model proposed in the DISS database, and the best-fitting solution derived from a seismological analysis performed by Lucente et al. [2005].

pictures.t: Intensities of the 1857 earthquake and R. Mallet route
pictures.c: The map shows the intensities of the 1857 earthquake superposed onto individual seismogenic sources from geological data and the source from intensity data (Boxer method). It shows also the route follewed by R. Mallet (from Burrato and Valensise [2008]).

pictures.t: Mallet's map with epicenter and damage pattern
pictures.c: Map showing the epicenter of the 1857 earthquake as it was calculated by R. Mallet. Note the striking correspondence among the epicenter, the damage distribution and the location of the DISS seismogenic sources (from Burrato and Valensise [2008]).

pictures.t: Felt area of the first shock of the 1857 earthquake
pictures.c: Map showing that the felt area of the strong foreshock of the 1857 earthquake well fit the position of the northern source (from Burrato and Valensise [2008]).

pictures.t: Scheme of ropture sequence of the 1857 earthquake
pictures.c: Scheme of the proposed sequence of rupture for the 1857 earthquake involving the activation of two adjoining sources (from Burrato and Valensise [2008]).
